attributes.body:
Like 'verb + ている', 'verb + てある' is a structure that will convey an ongoing state. However, てある may only be used with transitive verbs, and highlights the object itself as being the subject of the sentence (rather than the initial person/thing that performed the action).

As ある is being used, it highlights the object as being inanimate (or unable to undo the action that was performed on it). Due to this, てある is regularly translated as 'to be left (A)', or 'to remain (A)', where (A) is the original verb that somebody performed on the object.

Whether the sentence uses が or を to mark the object will depend on what is being emphasized. In cases where を is used, the emphasis is on the whoever performed the action, regardless of whether they are strictly mentioned in the sentence. However, が focuses more on the ongoing state of the object, without any emphasis being placed on the person who may have performed that action originally. Additionally, を may mark the object in sentences where the action itself involves some kind of preparation. For example:

予約（よやく） - Reservation (requires time investment to reserve).

準備（じゅんび） - Preparation (requires time investment to prepare).

録音（ろくおん） - Recording (requires time investment to make the recording).

In situations that involve no real preparation (opening a door, for example), が will be preferred when marking the object. This 'preparation' can be thought of as a time investment, where the invested time of the doer leads to the sentence more naturally expressing that person as the subject, and the object as what will take を.

attributes.source: [DBJG] A Dictionary of Basic Japanese Grammar

attributes.description: What's the difference between ～てある and ～た (past form)?

attributes.body: てある and まま(に) both describe continuing states, but differ in nuance. てある implies an action was done for a reason and that the result remains. For example, 窓が開けてある ('The window has been opened.') implies that it has been left open for a purpose. In contrast, まま(に) emphasizes that the state remains unchanged, without implying purpose, e.g. 窓を開けたまま家を出てしまった ('I left the house with the window open.').

attributes.body: Both てある and ておく express actions done for future purposes, but with key differences. てある focuses on the resulting state after the action is performed, e.g. 窓が開けてある ('The window has been opened.', when it remains open for some purpose). In contrast, ておく emphasizes the action itself, focusing on preparation, e.g. 窓を開けておいた ('I opened the window.', implying that it was for future benefit.). Note also the different particles used.

attributes.body: てある and っぱなし both describe ongoing states, but differ in tone. てある suggests something was done intentionally for future benefit. For example, 窓が開けてある means 'The window has been opened (for a reason).'. In contrast, っぱなし often implies carelessness. For example, 窓を開けっぱなしにして家を出た means 'I (carelessly) left the house with the window open.'.
